findings.summary: The Bundle, Then Compress flow has two bullets that each hold more than one idea, and the zip bullet mixes comparison facts.
findings.evidence: "gzip: fast, good ratio, default; xz: smaller, slower" and "zip compresses each file separately; opens on Windows and macOS"
findings.fix: Split each into one-idea bullets (one per tool), and keep the per-file zip point in the comparison table.

findings.summary: The interview point asks a question about zip access speed whose answer depends on a term not explained on the page, and the compare table gives no size or speed detail for .zip.
findings.evidence: "One file from zip faster? Per-file access; tar.gz decompresses from the start"
findings.fix: State in the bullets that tar.gz is one stream, so reading one file means decompressing from the start; zip can jump to a single entry.

findings.summary: The Create, List, Extract bullets bundle several ideas, and the code block is placed after bullets rather than introduced by one line.
findings.evidence: "-C dir extracts there; the folder must already exist" / "GNU tar auto-detects compression, so tar -xf works for .gz and .xz"
findings.fix: Put one idea per bullet, and give the code block a one-line lead-in before it.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "interview", "unpacking").
findings.evidence: Interview Point: Why does gzip delete the original file? How do you keep it? How do you search inside a .gz without unpacking? What does zip -r add that plain zip does not?
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The gzip/xz table has a redundant row and the commands are shown without a stated idea first; the zip commands are explained only by a trailing line.
findings.evidence: "Keep original | -k | -k" and "create, list, extract into out/" placed after the zip code block
findings.fix: Drop the duplicate row and mention -k once, and state each idea (create, list, extract) before the code, as comments on each line.

findings.summary: The Mistakes block combines two separate mistakes (gzip deleting originals, unzip scattering files) in one item.
findings.fix: Split into two mistakes, each with its own fix.

findings.summary: The Generate and Install notes mix several ideas in single bullets, and the commands are shown before the key idea is stated.
findings.evidence: "ssh-copy-id appends the key as one line to server ~/.ssh/authorized_keys" and "ssh-agent + ssh-add avoid retyping it" listed after the code
findings.fix: Give a one-line lead-in before the code (generate, install, connect), and split the passphrase and ssh-agent points into separate bullets.

findings.summary: The Mistakes block mixes unrelated mistakes under unclear headings, so a skimmer may not see which line is the mistake and which is the fix.
findings.evidence: "Before disabling passwords" followed by "Test ssh user@host with the key first, or you may lock yourself out."
findings.fix: Label the mistakes clearly, for example "Disabling passwords before testing the key", with the fix on its own line.

findings.summary: The scp vs rsync table packs a mixed cell and uses "same, swap the args" instead of a command, and the Port row mixes two flags in one cell.
findings.evidence: "Download | scp prod:/var/log/app.log . | same, swap the args" and "Port | -P (ssh uses -p) | from the alias"
findings.fix: Write the actual rsync download command, and move the -P versus -p note into its own bullet.

findings.summary: The rsync bullet "-a perms, times, recurse; -z compress; -n dry run; --delete removes extras" holds four ideas, and the dangerous --delete is not warned about.
findings.evidence: "-a perms, times, recurse; -z compress; -n dry run; --delete removes extras"
findings.fix: Split into one flag per bullet or a small flag table, and note that -n should be run before --delete.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet repeats the permissions table and trailing-slash note from page 5 with a small inconsistency (authorized_keys 600 only, versus 600 or 644 earlier).
findings.fix: Use the same value in both places, for example 600 (or 644).
